## My Thinking

I've been farming this same plot in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and corn, I grow wheat and corn, and that's what I'll grow again. The land here on the North China Plain is good for it, the market in the county town buys it, and I know how to do it. I'm 60 years old — this isn't the time to experiment.

I have about 10 mu of contracted land. In October I put in winter wheat, and as soon as the combine finishes in June I plant summer maize right behind it. Same 10 mu, two crops a year. That's how it works here.

For wheat I'll plough in autumn the way I always do — turns in the stubble, breaks up the hardpan. I use the Jimai variety that's been working well in this village for years. I'll apply base fertilizer before sowing — diammonium phosphate and some urea — and top-dress with urea at jointing. I irrigate four times: the pre-winter water in November to protect roots from freezing, jointing water in March, heading water in April, and grain-filling water in May. I spray herbicide in autumn after emergence, then fungicide and aphid spray in spring when the aphids come. Nothing fancy.

For maize I direct-seed right after wheat harvest, no-till, because there's no time. I buy hybrid seed — Zhengdan 958 or whatever the village agri-station is selling that works. Apply fertilizer at planting and again at the big bell stage. Maize gets rain in July and August but I'll still pump water twice — once at emergence if it's dry, once at silking. Spray herbicide early and watch for corn borer in summer.

I don't bother with potatoes or vegetables beyond the small patch by the house — my wife handles that. The wheat and maize are my income.
